opus-5.5.text:
I think the core intuition is that DNA is the fundamental layer of biology. Everything else, RNA, proteins, the regulatory machinery that decides when and where genes are turned on, is in some sense downstream of the genome. So if you want a model that actually understands biology, rather than just one slice of it, training on whole genomes gives you access to all of those layers at once.

A lot of the early excitement in AI for biology was around protein language models, and those have been incredibly powerful. But proteins don't exist in isolation. They're encoded in genes, those genes sit in a genomic context, and that context really matters. In bacteria, for example, functionally related genes are often clustered together in operons, and defense systems like CRISPR show up near specific neighbors. In more complex organisms you have enhancers, promoters, and noncoding regions that can sit very far from the genes they control. If you only ever look at protein sequences, you miss all of that.

So the bet is that if you train a model on raw nucleotide sequence at genome scale, with long enough context, it can start to learn the grammar of how these pieces fit together: which proteins interact, how RNA and protein co-function, how regulation is encoded. You're effectively learning from evolution's own record of billions of years of experiments, and you can do it across many species at once.

There's also a practical generative angle. If a model understands sequence at the level of whole systems, you can ask it to design not just a single protein but multi-component systems, like a CRISPR protein together with its guide RNA, or eventually much larger stretches of genetic circuitry. That moves us from predicting properties of individual molecules toward designing biology at the systems level.

The analogy I like is that DNA is the language biology is actually written in, and we're trying to build models that are fluent in it, not just in individual words but in paragraphs and chapters. We're still early, and there's a lot we don't understand about how much these models really capture versus pattern-match. But that's why genomes feel like such a compelling foundation to me.

r001.rationale: It describes DNA as the foundational layer and says genome-scale training exposes proteins, RNA, and regulatory machinery together, identifying genomes as a shared substrate for protein and non-protein components.

r002.rationale: It proposes training on raw nucleotide sequences at genome scale with long enough context to learn how components fit together, including protein interactions and RNA-protein co-function.

fable-5.1.text:
The thing I keep coming back to is that the genome is the only place in biology where we actually have the full recipe written down. Everything else we measure is a partial readout. RNA-seq tells you what's being transcribed in one cell type under one condition at one moment. Protein structures give you a snapshot of a folded molecule but nothing about when it gets made or what it's talking to. Those are all shadows of the same underlying object, and the underlying object is the DNA sequence.

So if you want a foundation model, in the real sense of something you can build lots of downstream things on top of, you want to train on the layer that everything else derives from. A genome encodes the proteins, but it also encodes the regulatory grammar, the promoters and enhancers, the splicing logic, the non-coding RNAs, the way genes are arranged relative to each other. All of that is sitting in the same string of A, C, G, T. A protein language model throws most of that away before training even starts.

The other argument is scale and diversity. Evolution has been running the experiment for us for billions of years across millions of species, and sequencing has gotten cheap enough that we've captured an enormous amount of that. Every genome is essentially a design that worked, that survived selection. When you train across bacteria, archaea, phage, eukaryotes, the model has to learn what's conserved and what's allowed to vary, and that's a very rich signal about function. Three billion base pairs for a human sounds large, but the full sequence space across the tree of life is where the interesting statistical structure lives.

And honestly, part of the motivation is that language models taught us a lesson. We used to think you needed to hand-engineer features, build a part-of-speech tagger, a parser, and so on. It turned out that if you just predict the next token on enough raw text, the structure emerges. DNA is literally a sequence of tokens with long-range dependencies. It would be strange if the same approach didn't work. So the bet is: train on the complete, unannotated genomic text, and let the model figure out what a gene is, what a regulatory element is, what a functional domain is, rather than us telling it in advance.

That's also what makes generation interesting rather than just prediction. If a model has learned the grammar at the whole-genome level, you can ask it to write new sequences, new proteins, new regulatory systems, eventually whole genomes, that obey rules we don't fully understand ourselves yet. That's a fundamentally different capability than annotating what's already there.

r001.rationale: The response says a genome encodes proteins as well as regulatory elements, splicing logic, non-coding RNAs, and gene arrangement in the same DNA sequence.

r002.rationale: It proposes training on complete genomes and notes long-range dependencies, but does not clearly say the model should learn interactions among genome-encoded molecular components.

astra-6.text:
I think whole genomes are compelling because they let you look at biology as a system. A gene’s function depends on its context—how it’s regulated, what other genes are present, and how those components work together. If you model individual genes in isolation, you miss a lot of those relationships.

Evolution has been exploring that space for billions of years. Every genome we observe is a result of that process, and comparing genomes gives us a way to learn which patterns are conserved, which can vary, and which changes tend to occur together. That’s a rich source of information for a model.

The exciting possibility is moving from recognizing those patterns to designing biological systems. But the genome isn’t the whole story: cells also depend on their environment and their history. So the question is how much we can learn from sequence, and then how we connect that to experiments that tell us what actually happens.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whole genomes, genes, and regulation, but does not identify genomes as a common encoding substrate for both protein and non-protein components.

r002.rationale: The response says models could learn genome patterns and relationships, but does not propose long-context models trained on genomes to learn interactions among genome-encoded molecular components.

sol-6.1.text:
I think whole genomes are compelling because they give you a shared language across biology. Every organism has to encode the instructions for building and maintaining itself in DNA. And evolution has been running experiments on those instructions for billions of years. The genomes we observe today are the outcomes of that process.

If you train a model on short fragments, you can learn a lot about local sequence patterns. But biology also depends on relationships across very long distances: how genes are regulated, how different genes work together, and how all of that fits into an organism. Whole genomes give you a chance to learn those relationships in context.

The exciting possibility is moving from recognizing patterns in DNA to being able to ask, “If I change this sequence, what happens?” And eventually, “What sequence would produce the function I want?” Whole genomes are a compelling starting point for that, although connecting sequence to function still requires experiments.

r001.rationale: It describes DNA as a shared language carrying instructions for organisms, but does not identify it as encoding both protein and non-protein components.

r002.rationale: It contrasts models trained on short fragments with whole-genome context and says this can reveal long-distance regulation and relationships among genes.
